S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, smoke, thermal runaway, evacuation, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 72 hours of learning of it, regardless of whether the incident was reported first through a customer, installer, or other channel. Affected customers must be notified within 5 business days when an event presents a safety risk or requires inspection, repair, or a change in use; urgent hazards require notice within 24 hours of determination.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, smoke, thermal runaway, evacuation, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 72 hours of learning of it, regardless of whether the incident was reported first through a customer, installer, or other channel. A complete incident report, including the model, circumstances, and known consequences, is due within 30 days. Affected customers must be notified within 5 business days when an event presents a safety risk or requires inspection, repair, or a change in use; urgent hazards require notice within 24 hours of determination. Manufacturers must maintain records, reconcile regulator reports with customer and service records, and submit an annual account of incidents and reporting completeness.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before sale and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and a representative sample. Results above 5% require prompt regulator review and a corrective-action plan with a timeline for follow-up testing; they do not automatically prohibit sale.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before sale and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and a representative sample. Manufacturers must provide complete per-model test results, including sample size and failure rate, to the relevant regulator and to customers purchasing that model. Before purchase, customers must receive the model’s actual test result and an explanation of the test and its limitations. Results above 5% require prompt regulator review and a corrective-action plan with a timeline for follow-up testing; they do not automatically prohibit sale. Regulators may require additional testing, corrective measures, or sales restrictions based on the results and associated risks.

S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression for units manufactured or first sold 36 months after this standard takes effect. The suppression system must be designed and validated to limit fire propagation and protect occupants and nearby property, using a regulator-approved test protocol. Manufacturers must provide installation, inspection, and maintenance instructions to customers and retain evidence of compliance for regulators.

Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of safety notices and corrective actions; urgent hazards require notice within 24 hours of determination, with other material safety notices within 5 business days. A manufacturer must initiate a regulator-supervised recall when any model exceeds 8 verified thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units during a calendar year. Calculate the rate using verified thermal incidents for that model and its installed-unit population during the same year. Manufacturers must reconcile incident records with customer reports and provide supporting records and calculations to regulators on request; incomplete reporting must not delay a safety response. The manufacturer must promptly notify regulators and affected customers with recall instructions. Regulators may require a recall or other corrective action for a serious hazard even below this threshold.

That exceeds the proposed 5% ceiling, so a fixed pass/fail cap could remove a currently marketed model without accounting for test uncertainty or corrective action. We recommend regulator review of results and a required corrective-action plan rather than automatic suspension of sales.

judge_section_notes: The final rules are a mixed outcome: S1 and S4 are within acceptable ranges, S5 is acceptable despite the recall trigger being exactly 8/100k (which would hit Halcyon's Ember 8), while S2 and S3 are weakened. S2 has a 5% review threshold but no automatic sales stop, and S3 sets a 24-month deadline for new units (beyond the 12-month acceptable limit) and a 6-year retrofit deadline. Northwind achieved its key goals: no public per-model disclosure, a 6-year retrofit, and no automatic sales ban for its Hearth 10; Halcyon secured customer test-result disclosure and a 36-month suppression deadline, but faces a mandatory recall for its Ember 8.
